summary: Registers the MIME types application/ISUP and application/QSIG so that telephone signaling messages can be carried inside SIP messages such as INVITE or INFO. This is useful when a SIP call is connected to the traditional telephone network. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3204 registers two MIME types so SIP messages can carry ISUP or QSIG telephone signaling data. The receiver can identify the data and decide what to do if it does not understand the type.

questions: how to carry isup in sip
what is the handling parameter in content-disposition
subtitle: MIME types that let SIP messages carry ISUP and QSIG telephone signaling data.

tldr.problem: When SIP connects a call to a telephone network, the SIP entities may need to carry ISUP or QSIG signaling data without changing it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3204 registers application/ISUP and application/QSIG as binary MIME types and defines version information and handling rules for unknown bodies.
tldr.outcome: The types are intended for signaling within a SIP session, not general transport. RFC 3204 was updated by RFC 3459 and RFC 5621.

today: RFC 3204 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2001. It was updated by RFC 3459 and RFC 5621, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why SIP Carries Telephone Signaling
sections.content:
ISUP carries signaling between telephone switches, and QSIG carries signaling between private branch exchanges. Some SIP calls need to carry these messages so telephone-network features can continue to work.

RFC 3204 registers MIME media types for carrying this data inside SIP messages. The document limits their use to signaling within a SIP session; it does not define general-purpose transport of circuit-network signaling. It also does not define how SIP and non-SIP systems negotiate compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP message may need to carry a telephone network's signaling data during a call. These MIME types label that data so the receiver can recognize it.

sections.title: Binary ISUP and QSIG Bodies
sections.content:
The ISUP and QSIG message bodies are binary data that SIP does not interpret. The RFC specifies binary encoding rather than Base64 because Base64 would add size and could require more processing.

application/ISUP requires a version parameter and may include a base parameter. The ISUP content begins at the Message Type Code, omitting the Routing Label and Circuit ID Code. application/QSIG has no required parameters and may include a version parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The SIP entity carries the signaling bytes without translating their contents. The ISUP type requires a version label; QSIG can include one to identify its variant.

sections.title: Version and Base Parameters
sections.content:
The version parameter identifies the version or variant that the receiver should parse. For ISUP, administrators choose its value. A base parameter can name a compatible base specification when a receiver does not recognize the version value.

For QSIG, the RFC lists iso as a version value for the cited ISO/IEC specifications. The default Content-Disposition type for both media types is signal, indicating signaling associated with the session rather than a description of the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Version labels tell a receiver which signaling format to expect. ISUP can also name a base format that the receiver may use.

sections.title: Handling Bodies a Receiver Cannot Read
sections.content:
The new handling parameter tells a SIP user agent server what to do when it does not understand a body type or disposition. If the value is optional, it MUST ignore the body. If the value is required, it MUST return 415 Unsupported Media Type. When the parameter is absent, required is assumed.

The RFC registers signal as a Content-Disposition type. It also sets rules for registering new version symbols: each symbol must point to a definitive specification, while symbols beginning with X- are for non-standard use and require bilateral agreement to cross administrative domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The handling parameter says whether an unknown body can be ignored or must cause an error. If no value is given, the receiver treats the body as required.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: ISUP and QSIG bodies may contain sensitive customer information. The RFC says encryption may be needed and points to SIP security mechanisms in RFC 2543 for protecting both the SIP message and its encapsulated signaling body.
sections.plainLanguage: The signaling body may contain private customer information. Protect it with the security mechanisms used for the SIP message when needed.
